reference.source: Royal College of Ophthalmologists guidance / Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Age-related separation of the posterior vitreous cortex from the internal limiting membrane of the retina, driven by vitreous liquefaction (synchysis) and weakening of vitreoretinal adhesion
Classic symptoms are the sudden onset of floaters together with flashing lights (photopsia) from vitreoretinal traction, often more noticeable in dim light or with eye movement
A Weiss ring, the detached annulus of condensed vitreous from around the optic disc, is effectively pathognomonic when seen
The principal danger is that traction may create a retinal tear, which can progress to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; a meaningful proportion of symptomatic acute PVDs have a tear at presentation
Pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous, described as tobacco dust or Shafer's sign, strongly suggest a retinal break and mandate careful peripheral examination
Accompanying vitreous haemorrhage substantially raises the likelihood of a retinal tear and should prompt urgent, thorough retinal assessment

All symptomatic patients need dilated fundus examination with scleral indentation; those with an initially normal examination warrant safety-netting and often repeat review because breaks can appear later
Risk is increased in myopia, after cataract surgery, following trauma, and in the fellow eye of a patient who has had a PVD-related tear or detachment
reference.pathophysiology: With ageing the vitreous gel undergoes liquefaction (synchysis) while the adhesion between the posterior vitreous cortex and the internal limiting membrane weakens. When liquefied vitreous passes through a dehiscence in the posterior cortex into the retrohyaloid space, the cortex peels away from the retina, producing a posterior vitreous detachment. Where focal vitreoretinal adhesions persist, for example at the vitreous base, along retinal vessels or at areas of lattice degeneration, dynamic traction during separation can tear the retina or avulse a vessel, causing a retinal break and/or vitreous haemorrhage. Photopsiae arise from mechanical stimulation of the retina by this traction, while floaters reflect condensed vitreous and the Weiss ring casting shadows on the retina.
additionalDifferentials: Retinal tear or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Vitreous haemorrhage from other causes such as proliferative retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion or a retinal macroaneurysm
Retinal migraine or cortical or occipital photopsia
Posterior uveitis or vitritis producing floaters
Ocular ischaemia or other retinal cause of photopsia
additionalInvestigations: Dilated slit-lamp biomicroscopy with peripheral retinal examination and scleral indentation
Assessment for Shafer's sign (pigment in the anterior vitreous)
B-scan ultrasonography when the fundus view is obscured, for example by vitreous haemorrhage, to detect PVD, tears or detachment
OCT to demonstrate a Weiss ring, vitreomacular traction or coexisting macular pathology
Documented visual acuity and confrontation or formal visual field assessment
Repeat examination after an interval, or sooner if new symptoms develop, to detect delayed retinal breaks
redFlags: A curtain, shadow or progressive field defect suggesting retinal detachment
A sudden shower of floaters or vitreous haemorrhage indicating a probable retinal tear
Tobacco dust (Shafer's sign) in the anterior vitreous
Progressive increase in floaters or flashes, or any loss of central vision
reference.prognosis: An uncomplicated posterior vitreous detachment is benign, and symptoms usually diminish over weeks to months as floaters settle and the patient adapts. The overall prognosis depends on prompt detection and treatment of any associated retinal tear, which when treated early usually prevents progression to detachment.
pitfalls: Failing to perform, or to repeat, an adequate peripheral retinal examination with indentation and so missing a retinal break
Discharging a patient with a vitreous haemorrhage without excluding a tear or arranging timely follow-up
Ignoring new or changing symptoms after an initially normal examination
Attributing all floaters to benign PVD without considering uveitis, haemorrhage or detachment
references: Royal College of Ophthalmologists guidance on posterior vitreous detachment and retinal detachment
